content: The percentage of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza (P&I) peaked between weeks 3 and 10 of the influenza season. During the 1999-2000 season, P&I mortality exceeded the epidemic threshold for 20 out of 21 weeks from October 3, 1999, to February 26, 2000. Since October 3, 1999, laboratories collaborating with the World Health Organization and the National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System in the United States tested 73,576 respiratory specimens for influenza viruses, of which 12,651 (17%) were positive. For the week ending February 26, 2000, 111 out of 1,118 specimens (10%) tested positive for influenza. The highest percentage of specimens testing positive for influenza during the season was 33%, observed in the week ending December 25, 1999 (week 51). In the previous five influenza seasons, peak percentages of positive specimens ranged from 19% to 34%, with peak weeks occurring between week 51 and week 6. Among the influenza A viruses subtyped as of February 26, 2000, 99% were H3N2 viruses, and 1% were H1N1 viruses. Influenza activity in the United States increased significantly in mid-December 1999 and appeared to peak between the weeks ending December 25, 1999 (week 51), and January 15, 2000 (week 2). The predominant viruses isolated this season were influenza A (H3N2) viruses, antigenically similar to those that have predominated since the 1997-1998 season and were well-matched to the season's vaccine. The percentage of patient visits for influenza-like illness (ILI) peaked at 6% during the week ending January 1, 2000 (week 52). In the previous five influenza seasons (1994-1995 through 1998-1999), peak percentages of ILI visits ranged from 5% to 7%, with peak weeks occurring between week 50 and week 7. For the week ending February 26, 2000, one state epidemiologist reported widespread influenza activity, and 10 reported regional activity. The highest combined number of reports of either widespread or regional influenza activity by state and territorial epidemiologists was 44 during the week ending January 15, 2000 (week 2). In the previous five influenza seasons, the highest total number of such reports during any week ranged from 25 to 46, with peak weeks occurring between week 1 and week 10. The 122 Cities Mortality Reporting System (MRS) indicated that the peak percentage of deaths attributed to P&I this season was higher than levels observed during the previous five seasons. The 122 Cities MRS is a voluntary mortality reporting system that provides weekly data to estimate the percentage of total deaths attributed to P&I. Factors influencing the percentage of P&I deaths include the incidence of influenza in the population, pre-existing immunity levels, the virulence of circulating influenza viruses, the proportion of the population at high risk for complications, the incidence and virulence of other respiratory pathogens, and methodological factors. A change in the P&I case definition for the 122 Cities MRS contributed to the increased percentage of P&I deaths reported this season. Before the 1999-2000 season, deaths were classified as P&I deaths if pneumonia was listed in part I of the death certificate or if influenza was listed anywhere on the certificate. The new case definition, implemented for the 1999-2000 season, classified deaths as P&I deaths if either pneumonia or influenza was listed anywhere on the death certificate. This simpler definition is more compatible with computerized mortality systems. The concurrent change from ICD-9 to ICD-10 coding for underlying causes of death also impacted reporting. CDC will continue to analyze data from the 122 Cities MRS and compare it with vital statistics data to clarify the effects of these changes. Influenza surveillance data collected by the CDC are updated weekly from October through May. Summary reports are available through the CDC's voice information system and other channels.
